reviews.overall: **Nhận xét bài tập về nhà.** Em đã viết đủ bốn đoạn, chọn đúng ba nước và chia phần chi tiết tại mốc 2006; các xu hướng chính của Argentina và Australia cũng đúng. Tuy nhiên, số ô tô của Thailand năm 2006 là 1,162,356, không phải 1,167,356. Em còn nhận xét Australia thấp nhất trong toàn bảng, trong khi Argentina năm 2003 mới là ô có số thấp nhất. Cô yêu cầu em kiểm tra lại từng ô số liệu, nêu rõ diễn biến của Thailand trong Overview và sửa cách dùng “amount of cars”, động từ ở câu cuối.
reviews.dataGrouping: Em chia Detail 1 cho giai đoạn 2003–2006 và Detail 2 cho 2006–2009; mốc giữa này giúp so sánh ba nước và đúng với diễn biến của bảng. Mỗi đoạn đều có hơn hai câu. Ở Overview, em nên nói rõ Thailand đạt đỉnh vào 2006 rồi giảm, thay vì chỉ viết chung rằng số xe tăng rồi giảm.

The table illustrates how many cars were manufactured in Argentina, Australia and Thailand over a 6-year period commencing from 2003.
​Overall, there was a general increase in the figures for cars made in Argentina, while an opposite trend was observed in Australia. The figures for Thailand went up and down. Also of note is that it consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.
​To elaborate, in 2003, 452,163 cars were produced in Australia with a drop to 341,268 cars in 2006. The figures for Argentina and Thailand, conversely, grew from 235,088 and 735,852 to 352,759 and 1,167,356 cars during the same period of time. The number of cars in Thailand marked the highest point of the entire chart.
​Regarding the latter half of the provided timeline, the amount of cars in Argentina continued to go up, reaching 466,089 cars in 2009. By contrast, the figures for Australia and Thailand fell to 245,624 and 999,963 cars, respectively. The number of cars in Australia was obviously the lowest over the whole graph. In Thailand, the production of cars are still ranking first on the entire chart.

reviews.overall: Em đã viết đúng đề, đủ độ dài và chia hai đoạn Detail theo nam, nữ hợp lý. Tuy nhiên, Overview chưa cho thấy số tù nhân nam giảm đầu kỳ rồi mới tăng, còn số nữ chạm đáy năm 1941 và dao động sau đó. Ở Detail, biểu đồ chỉ cho biết số người đang ở tù, không cho biết số người bị bắt; em cũng bỏ qua bước tăng mạnh của nam từ 1971 đến 1981. Bài này em soát chưa kỹ: một câu thiếu mệnh đề chính, một câu nối động từ với danh từ không song song và một số dạng động từ sai. Cô yêu cầu em sửa rồi nộp lại.
reviews.dataGrouping: Em chia Detail theo nam và nữ; cách chia này phù hợp vì hai đường không có cùng một mốc giữa kỳ nổi bật. Đoạn nam nên nối mốc đầu, đáy 1931, giai đoạn gần 20.000 và bước nhảy 1971–1981 với mốc cuối. Đoạn nữ nên cho thấy đáy 1941, mức hồi năm 1961, lần giảm năm 1971 và mức cuối vẫn thấp hơn đầu kỳ.

It is clear that the male prison population was much higher than the female prison population throughout the period.

After, the female prison population was declined to 800 prisoners before upturn gradually to end at around 2,000 prisoners in the same period of time.

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The two line charts compare the numbers of male and female prisoners in a European country from 1911 to 2001.

Overall, men consistently accounted for far more prisoners than women. The male prison population fell in the early decades before recovering and rising sharply after 1971. By contrast, the female population dropped steeply to a low in 1941, fluctuated thereafter, and ended below its initial level.

The number of male prisoners was approximately 18,000 in both 1911 and 1921, before falling to about 10,000 in 1931. It then recovered to nearly 20,000 by 1951 and remained close to that level until 1971. A particularly large increase followed: the figure reached roughly 39,000 in 1981 and continued to rise to around 46,000 by 2001.

Among women, the prisoner count declined from about 3,200 in 1911 to roughly 500 in 1941. It subsequently climbed to approximately 1,500 in 1961, then fell back to around 700 in 1971. From that point, it rose to about 1,900 by 2001, which was still well below the figure at the start of the period.

​Overall, the amount of different kinds of meat were used rate decreased in beef, lamb and fish; with beef recording the most pronounced decline. ​Regarding categories with lower data, the intake of lamb in an European country also dropped from 150 grams to 50 grams between 1979 and 2004. reviews.suggestedRevision:
The line graph compares weekly consumption of chicken, beef, lamb and fish, measured in grams per person, in a European country between 1979 and 2004.

Overall, chicken consumption rose markedly and overtook beef around 1989, becoming the highest by the end of the period. By contrast, beef and lamb declined substantially, while fish remained the least consumed category and fell only slightly overall.

In 1979, each person ate about 140 grams of chicken per week, compared with roughly 220 grams of beef. Chicken consumption fluctuated slightly as it climbed, passing beef at about 200 grams in the late 1980s and reaching approximately 250 grams in 2004. Beef, meanwhile, peaked at around 240 grams in the early 1980s before falling, with some fluctuations, to about 110 grams per person per week in the final year.

Regarding the two categories with lower figures, lamb consumption dropped from around 150 to approximately 55 grams per person per week, despite a few small recoveries. Fish consumption was far lower than that of lamb throughout; it moved from about 60 grams in 1979 to roughly 35 grams in 2004, a much smaller decline than those seen for beef and lamb.

​Overall, there was a general increase in the share of women serving in parliament in all five countries over the period. Notably, the figure for Italy consistently had the highest figures by 2012.  
​To elaborate, in 2000, the percentage of female members of parliament in Germany stood at 34% and rose slightly to 37% in 2012. The figure for Italy witnessed signs of growth, going up from 26% to 39%, marking the highest point of the entire chart. France's figures shared a different pattern, climbing sharply to peak of 36% in 2004, before declining to around 30% in the final year. Also of note is that Germany, Italy and France consistently recorded higher figures than others.  
​Regarding the remaining countries, the share of women serving in parliament in Belgium also grew to from 17% to 28% between 2000 and 2012. The figures for the UK, likewise, increased significantly by 24% after 12 years. These data, however, eventually matching Belgium's figures and still remained far below those of Germany, Italy and France.

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The pie charts illustrate how students' reasons for choosing a university in the UK were distributed in 1997 and 2007.

Overall, the percentages citing suitable degree courses, proximity to parental home and quality of teaching rose, whereas those citing quality of resources and good sports and social activities fell. Suitable degree courses remained the leading reason in both years. Proximity to parental home was the least cited reason in 1997, while good sports and social activities ranked last in 2007.

To elaborate, in 1997, 35% of students selected the university for its suitable degree courses, with a slight rise in this figure to 37% in 2007. By contrast, the proportion citing the quality of resources declined from 21% to 17% over the same period.

Regarding the remaining reasons, the proportion of students choosing the university for its proximity to their parents' homes more than doubled, from 10% in 1997 to 22% in 2007, the largest rise. The figure for quality of teaching also grew, though only from 15% to 18%. In contrast, the share selecting the university for its good sports and social activities dropped from 19% to 6%, the largest decline and the lowest figure in 2007.

The given table chart illustrates the proportion of the population aged 65 and above in three major countries from 1988 to 2000 and predictions until 2030.
​Overall, it is expected that there will be an increase in the percentages of people aged 65 and over in all three countries. Equally notably, Germany's figures records the highest figures throughout the surveyed years.
​To elaborate, in 1988, Germany started at the leading position of the entire chart at 20,35%, and its share of the population aged 65 and above went up progressively by about 5% after 12 years. The figures for Canada, likewise, grew from 16,45% to 20,65% during the same period. The UK's figures also increased slightly from 14,25% to 14,80% between 1988 and 2000.
​Regarding the latter half of the period, the percentages of the population aged 65 and over in Germany is anticipated to grow significantly to 30,65%, marking the highest point of the entire chart in 2030. The figures for Canada and the UK are projected to witness an upturn from 20,65% and 14,80% to 26,35% and 20,45% respectively. The proportion of elderly people in the UK is predicted to remain far below those of Canada and Germany.

The table compares the shares of residents aged 65 or over in Canada, Germany and the UK in 1988 and 2000, and gives a projection for 2030.

Overall, the proportion of older residents rose in every country between 1988 and 2000 and is expected to continue rising by 2030. Germany records the highest percentage in all three years, while the UK remains the lowest; Canada's figures lie between them.

In 1988, 20.35% of Germany's population was aged 65 or over, compared with 16.45% in Canada and 14.25% in the UK. By 2000, the German figure had risen to 25.53%, a gain of 5.18 percentage points. Canada's share also grew to 20.65%, whereas the UK recorded only a slight increase to 14.80%.

From 2000 to 2030, Germany's proportion is projected to rise further to 30.65%, the highest value in the table. Canada's figure is expected to reach 26.35%, with that for the UK rising to 20.45%. The proportion of elderly people in the UK is predicted to remain far below those of Canada and Germany.
